target_length: 12-18 minutes of reading (~2,600-4,000 words), targeting about 15 minutes (~3,300 words)
note: Logan's instruction of 2026-09-25: a complete restart of the Daily Learning Brief, replacing the 150-day curriculum and the planned year two outright (retired, not continued -- see docs/SPEC.md Sec.0c). Fifteen subjects outside his main Finance/Economics/Accounting education, twenty weekday lessons each, run strictly in sequence with no interleaving -- Mathematics finishes entirely before Physics starts, and so on. The goal is a very strong general baseline across each field, not mastery: the 20% of ideas that give 80% of the understanding, pitched at an intelligent, curious reader with no formal background in the subject. Each subject's scope is fixed to avoid duplicating another subject's territory (see each block's mission). No quizzes, no problem sets, no spaced repetition. No audio (Logan, 2026-09-25).

phases.name: Mathematics
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of algebra and functions, Euclidean geometry and trigonometry, calculus (limits, derivatives, integrals), linear algebra (vectors and matrices), probability and statistics, and discrete mathematics and logic — not mastery, but a strong baseline for recognizing these ideas wherever they appear.

phases.name: Physics
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of Newtonian mechanics (forces, energy, momentum), thermodynamics, waves, electricity and magnetism, relativity, quantum mechanics, and nuclear physics. The goal is a strong intellectual baseline for following science and engineering conversations, not a physics degree.

phases.name: Rockets, Spaceflight & Astronomy
phases.mission: By the end of this block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of how rockets reach orbit (thrust, the rocket equation, staging, propellants), how orbits and interplanetary trajectories work (Kepler's laws, vis-viva, Hohmann transfers, gravity assists), how humans live, travel, and return from space (life support, reentry, Apollo, modern stations), and the architecture of the universe itself (stars, galaxies, cosmology) — not mastery, a strong baseline.

phases.name: AI, Computing & Modern Technology
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of how computers physically and logically work, how software and operating systems organize them, how networks and the internet move information, the history and mechanics of AI from symbolic rules through neural networks to today's Transformer-based large language models, and the modern technology landscape of cloud computing, AI compute, and cybersecurity — not mastery, a strong baseline for following any tech conversation or headline.

phases.name: Psychology
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of psychology's major schools of thought, research methods (including the replication crisis), sensation and perception, learning and memory, cognitive and social development, personality, emotion and motivation, and the classic social-psychology findings on obedience, conformity, and bias — not mastery, a strong baseline for recognizing these concepts in everyday life, media, and later subjects.

phases.name: Philosophy
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of logic and argument, the major epistemological positions on knowledge and skepticism, the core metaphysical questions of reality, causation, free will, and identity, the mind-body problem, the three major ethical frameworks and the realism/anti-realism debate in metaethics, the foundational ideas of political philosophy, the classic arguments in philosophy of religion and philosophy of science, and the arc of Western philosophy from Socrates through existentialism — not mastery, a strong baseline.

phases.name: Chemistry
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of how atoms are built and organized on the periodic table, how they bond into ionic, covalent, and metallic structures, how reactions are balanced and quantified through stoichiometry, how matter behaves as gas, liquid, and solid, how acids, bases, and solutions work, how energy flows through reactions, and why carbon's unique bonding underlies both synthetic materials and the biology coming next. This is a strong working baseline, not mastery -- enough to read a nutrition label, a battery spec sheet, or a climate report with real understanding.

phases.name: Biology
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of the cell as life's basic unit, DNA and heredity, evolution by natural selection, how the major body systems function, reproduction and development, ecology and ecosystems, biodiversity and classification, and modern biotechnology (CRISPR, vaccines, genetic engineering) — not mastery, a strong baseline for following any biology-related news, book, or conversation.

phases.name: Engineering
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of the engineering design process, statics and structural engineering (trusses, beams, arches, skyscrapers), materials science, mechanical engineering (heat engines, machines), electrical engineering (circuits and the power grid), control systems and feedback, and systems engineering and reliability -- illustrated throughout by real landmark projects and failures. Not mastery: a strong baseline for recognizing how any real-world built system was actually designed, and why.

phases.name: History & Civilizations
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a causal, globally balanced map of world history: the first civilizations and the great religious and philosophical traditions they produced, the medieval trade and conquest networks (Islamic, Mongol, Silk Road, African, Mesoamerican) that first tied much of the world together, and the modern pivot of 1492, industrialization, empire, the World Wars, and the Cold War that built the borders, institutions, and rivalries of today. This is a strong working baseline for understanding how the present world came to be, not mastery.

phases.name: Geography & Earth Science
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of the major pillars of physical geography: plate tectonics and the rock cycle that build and reshape Earth's surface; the atmosphere, oceans, and climate system that drive weather and long-term climate change; and the erosional landforms, biomes, and natural resources that result. Not mastery — a strong baseline for recognizing why physical geography shapes where people live, what they can grow or extract, and the stage on which later subjects like geopolitics will play out.

phases.name: Government & Law
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of the state and sovereignty, the major architectures of government (presidential/parliamentary, federal/unitary, democratic/authoritarian), constitutionalism and separation of powers, how legislatures, executives, bureaucracies and courts actually function, the common-law/civil-law legal traditions, rights, electoral systems, and how legitimacy and the rule of law hold governments together or fail — not mastery, a strong practical baseline for reading news, history and law intelligently.

phases.name: Geopolitics & International Relations
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of the international system and its rival theoretical lenses (realism, liberalism, constructivism), the sources and instruments of state power (military, economic, soft), the mechanisms of security — alliances, deterrence, and nuclear strategy — and the institutions that manage cooperation and conflict (UN, WTO, IMF, EU). He will also understand the leading theories of why wars start and end, the tools of economic statecraft, and enough of today's great-power competition and regional flashpoints to read geopolitical news as an analyst, not a spectator — not mastery, a strong baseline.

phases.name: Sociology & Anthropology
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of sociology's three major theoretical lenses (functionalism, conflict theory, symbolic interactionism), the core social institutions and processes that organize any society (socialization, family, religion, education, stratification, race, gender, deviance, organizations, and social change), and anthropology's comparative toolkit (cultural relativism, kinship, cultural variation, and the deep timeline of human prehistory). This is a strong general baseline for recognizing these concepts in the news, in institutions, and in everyday social life — not academic mastery.

phases.name: Communication, Media & Linguistics
phases.mission: By the end of this 20-lesson block, Logan will have a working conceptual grasp of how language itself works (sound, grammar, and meaning), how human communication and media evolved from oral tradition through print, broadcast, and the internet, and how rhetoric, information theory, and journalism structure the flow of information. He will also understand the real mechanisms behind propaganda, misinformation, and today's algorithm-driven media landscape — not mastery of linguistics or media studies, but a strong baseline for reading, listening, and thinking critically about any information he encounters, closing out the Academy.

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Numbers, infinity, and the birth of proof
days.headline_hint: The number that broke a cult: how the square root of 2 shattered the Pythagoreans' worldview
days.focus: Traces how the number system grew from counting (naturals) to integers, fractions, and finally the irrational and real numbers, and introduces mathematical proof as the method that establishes something is true forever, not just probably true.
days.model_or_equation: proof by contradiction (the irrationality of the square root of 2)

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Algebra: variables, equations, and solving for the unknown
days.headline_hint: The 9th-century Baghdad scholar who taught the world to solve for x
days.focus: Introduces algebra as the leap from arithmetic with specific numbers to reasoning about unknowns in general, covering how to solve linear and quadratic equations and why al-Khwarizmi's work still names the field.

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Functions: the language of change and relationship
days.headline_hint: One idea that secretly runs your GPS, your thermostat, and your streaming recommendations: the function
days.focus: Presents the function, a rule that turns one quantity into another, as the central organizing idea of the rest of mathematics, covering notation, graphs, domain and range, and linear versus nonlinear behavior.

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Euclidean geometry: axioms, proof, and the logic of space
days.headline_hint: The 2,300-year-old rulebook for space that still frames every blueprint and satellite orbit
days.focus: Covers Euclid's axiomatic method, building an entire system of geometry from a handful of self-evident starting rules, and the core toolkit of points, angles, triangles, congruence, and the Pythagorean theorem.

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Trigonometry: triangles, circles, and periodic motion
days.headline_hint: Why the same math that measures a pyramid's shadow also describes a sound wave
days.focus: Extends geometry to the relationships between a triangle's angles and sides, then reframes sine and cosine on the unit circle as the mathematical language of anything that repeats: waves, cycles, and rotation.
days.model_or_equation: sine and cosine on the unit circle

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Exponents and logarithms: the mathematics of growth and scale
days.headline_hint: Why a pandemic, a chain reaction, and a bacteria colony all obey the same curve
days.focus: Explains exponential growth and decay and their inverse, the logarithm, showing why so much of nature shares one mathematical shape, and why scientists measure some things, like earthquakes and sound, on log scales.
days.model_or_equation: y = a times b^x and its inverse, the logarithm

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Complex numbers: extending the number line into a plane
days.headline_hint: The 'imaginary' number mathematicians once mocked, now essential to every circuit and signal
days.focus: Introduces the imaginary unit i and the complex plane as a natural extension of the number system, born from trying to solve equations like x squared equals negative one, closing the loop opened on Day 1.

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Sequences, series, and taming infinity
days.headline_hint: The paradox that says Achilles can never catch the tortoise, and the math that resolves it
days.focus: Covers arithmetic and geometric sequences and series, showing how infinitely many terms can add up to a finite number, which resolves Zeno's ancient paradox of motion and sets up the idea of a limit.
days.model_or_equation: sum of an infinite geometric series

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: The limit: approaching forever without arriving
days.headline_hint: The idea that let mathematicians finally trust infinity, and unlocked calculus
days.focus: Formalizes the limit, what a function approaches as its input gets arbitrarily close to some value, as the rigorous foundation that resolved centuries of unease about infinity and makes calculus possible.
days.model_or_equation: the formal definition of a limit

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: The derivative: the mathematics of instantaneous change
days.headline_hint: How Newton and Leibniz taught the world to measure change at a single instant
days.focus: Introduces the derivative as the slope of a curve at a point, the rate of change of one quantity with respect to another, built directly from the limit, and previews why it becomes the workhorse of physics, engineering, and modern AI.

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: The integral and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
days.headline_hint: The other half of calculus: how adding up infinitely many slices gives an exact area
days.focus: Covers the integral as the accumulation of a quantity, the area under a curve, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, which reveals that integration and differentiation are inverse operations, the result that unifies calculus.

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Differential equations: writing down how things change
days.headline_hint: The equations that don't solve for a number, they solve for a whole future
days.focus: Introduces the differential equation, an equation involving a rate of change, as the way mathematicians describe systems that evolve over time, from cooling coffee to population growth, without yet needing specific solving techniques.

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Vectors: quantities with direction
days.headline_hint: Why 'how fast' is only half the answer, and 'which way' is the other half
days.focus: Introduces the vector, a quantity with both magnitude and direction, along with vector addition and components, the essential language for describing forces and motion that recurs constantly from here forward.

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Matrices and linear transformations
days.headline_hint: The grid of numbers that can rotate a galaxy simulation or rank every page on the internet
days.focus: Extends vectors to matrices, rectangular arrays of numbers that transform space by rotating, scaling, or stretching it, introducing matrix multiplication and the linear-algebra habit of handling many numbers as a single object.
days.model_or_equation: a matrix as a linear transformation

days.subject: Mathematics
days.topic: Probability: the mathematics of uncertainty

days.focus: Introduces probability theory, born from 17th-century gamblers' questions, covering outcomes, events, independence, and conditional probability as the formal language for reasoning about uncertainty.

days.subject: Mathematics
